facing._deadZone: How much sideways drift counts as noise before a unit turns round. Raised from 0.15 when the map was re-traced: the old lane never really went west and its steepest leg drifted 3px over 92, or 0.03 of its length. The new road genuinely bends back on itself, and its steepest leg drifts 14.5px west while dropping 69.6 — 0.20. At 0.15 that flipped an enemy round to walk down the hill backwards and then flipped it back.

cancel._note: CANCEL's own colours. It is the way out of a mode the player may have entered by accident, so it is the loudest control on the screen rather than the quietest: a warm red slab with a cream glyph and label, not the grey wash it was. The wash read as disabled chrome, which is most of why playtesting reported it as unfindable before it was reported as dead.
cancel.label: CANCEL

layout._startWidth: THE WAVE BANNER, and it is much smaller than it was. At 240x44 it carried `WAVE 2 · 3s · +4` and, mid-wave, `The Gathering · 6 left` -- a wave name that told the player nothing they could act on and a countdown they could not change. With the name and the seconds gone the longest string it ever has to hold is `START WAVE 13`, so the plate is sized to that. 44 stays as the height because it is the minimum tap target and this is a button.

hud._bossBarWidth: Read at last. It was 560 and unread: drawBossBar took layout.messageRow.width instead, which is 563px on an 844px screen — 67% of the width for one wave in thirteen. 300 is wide enough to read a health fraction off and narrow enough to stay a bar rather than a band. The message row still bounds it, so a narrow phone shrinks the bar rather than pushing it into the counters.
hud._bossBarTop: DELETED. It said 10 and nothing read it: the bar sits in the message row, which the layout places, so a second opinion about its y could only ever disagree with the layout. It is centred in that row now.

heroChip._note: THE HERO'S PORTRAIT AND HEALTH, at the bottom beside the ability buttons. It replaces the wide bar that used to sit under the counters at the top left, which drew the hero's health in a second place -- the sprite on the map already had a bar over its head -- and put a solid plate across the top of the board for the whole run. The two readouts are one now: the bar is drawn ON the portrait rather than beside it, so the thing that says how the hero is doing is the thing with the hero's face on it.
heroChip._size: The chip's square edge, and it is a TAP TARGET: tapping it selects the hero, and the next tap on the map moves him. 60 clears the 44pt minimum with room to spare, which matters more here than for the ability buttons beside it -- a mis-tap on those wastes a cooldown, and a mis-tap on this walks the hero into a fireball.
heroChip._gap: Between the chip and the nearest ability button, and it is deliberately LARGER than the 26px seam between the drafted group and the hero medallions is wide at the edges -- the two controls do different things and a thumb travelling along the row must not find them adjacent. Checked at 375x667 by the harness, which is where the row is tightest.
heroChip._barHeight: The health bar, overlaid across the bottom of the portrait rather than placed beside it. Thin, because it is read as a colour and a length rather than as a shape, and because the portrait underneath it is what the chip is for.
heroChip._downTint: A hero who is down: the portrait desaturated to this and the bar replaced by the respawn countdown. The state has to be legible at a glance from the bottom of the screen, because it is the answer to 'why is nothing happening where I left him'.

towerTier._pipBaselineOffset: Where the tier row sits relative to the tower's base, in world pixels: negative is up into the art, positive is down onto the grass. It was pipDropBelowBase: 9, which put the whole row clear of the foot and reading as a separate object on the ground. 0 straddles the base line so the row belongs to the tower.

buildPad._quietScreenWidth: The flagstone in SCREEN pixels across, at the default camera zoom — the unit it was asked for in, and the only one that means anything for a thing you look at. The world width falls out of it (90 / defaultZoom), so changing the zoom band does not silently resize the pad. It also lands where the art was cut for: at 90 screen px the slab is about 40 world px tall, and CLAUDE.md rule 7 wants 40 x 2.37 x 3 = 284 source pixels against the 272 delivered.

loadout._cardProbeHeight: A nominal card height, used only to ask the painted frame for its inset while MEASURING how tall a card needs to be. The inset barely varies with height and the real one is used when the card is drawn; this exists so the measurement has something to ask.
loadout._floors: The least each block may be squeezed to before the screen scrolls instead. heroMinHeight is solved through the hero row rather than applied to it, so the block still reports what it needs at that ceiling; cardMinHeight is a flat floor for a dealt card.
loadout._scrollFadeHeight: How tall the fade along the bottom of the content band is when the stack overflows and scrolls. It is the affordance: a card clipped by a hard invisible edge reads as a broken screen, one that dissolves reads as more content.

copy.drawnAtRandom: Towers and specials are drawn at random. Pick your hero.

loadout._buttonGap: Between the two buttons. It was in this file and unread: the row was laid out from two hardcoded offsets and the gap they happened to leave was 10.
loadout._buttonPadX: Inside a button, either side of its label. Both buttons take the width the WIDER label needs, so the row is symmetrical.
loadout._rowShares: HOW THE TWO DEALT ROWS SPLIT WHAT THE HERO BLOCK DID NOT TAKE. There used to be a third share here, for the hero, and it was the biggest -- a fixed 40% whether the content wanted it or not. The picker inside absorbed the difference by subtraction and went negative on a short screen, which threw the portraits out of the card and over the heading. The hero block is sized to its content now, under `heroSectionMaxShare`, so it has no share to hold.

heroCard._note: One hero's plate in the picker. It had none: the tiles were bare portraits on the panel, which is why the row read as a filmstrip rather than as five cards. Selection is the plate lightening AND a ring AND a tick, three signals, because this is the one control on the screen that changes what the run is.

heroRow._note: THE HERO PICKER, as a row of proper cards. It was a strip of tiles whose height was whatever was left after the description had taken 42% of the panel -- which went negative on a short screen and threw the portraits out of the card and over the heading. The row is sized to its content now and the section is sized to the row; see systems/HeroRow.ts. minPortrait is a HARD floor with a consequence: below it the row wraps to two lines rather than shrinking, because five 24px smudges are not a picker.

heroDescription._note: The blurb beside the hero's two buttons. The panel used to be three lines at the top of a tall empty box; the space is used now.

loadout._heroSectionMaxShare: The ceiling on what the hero block may take out of the three-row budget before the towers and the specials get theirs. The block asks for what its content needs; this is what stops a long blurb starving the two rows underneath it.

iconFallback._note: Drawn in place of a UI icon whose file is missing. Deliberately wrong-looking: the layout holds and the button works, but nobody mistakes it for finished art.

heroFrames._note: The hero clips. impactFrame is 1-based to match the filenames, and the damage fires on it rather than when the swing starts.
heroFrames._walkFps: Arithmetic, not taste. Cory moves at 104 world px/s and renders 78.8 world px tall. A 4-frame cycle is two steps, so at 12fps that is 3 cycles a second and 17.3px per step — 0.22 body-heights, against a human stride of 0.4-0.45. His feet were taking steps half the length his speed demanded, which is what sliding is. At 6fps it is 34.7px per step, 0.44 body-heights.
heroFrames._attackFps: Kept at 12, and separate from the walk for a reason: impactFrame is the third frame, so one shared rate would have moved the swing's landing from 167ms to 333ms. Halving the walk to fix a slide must not double the attack telegraph.

ring._note: The one tower menu: a radial ring of icon buttons around the pad or tower, and a description panel beside it. Every number is in CSS pixels and stays that size at every camera zoom — the ring is HUD chrome positioned by projecting a world point, not a world object.
ring._buttonSize: The plate. iconSize is the floor, not this: 40px of icon needs a plate bigger than 40 to sit on, and 50 leaves a 5px border. It is not larger because a notched 568x320 leaves a 171px strip between the counters and the ability bar, and six options need 2*50 plus the price badge inside it. The exhaustive placement test pinned that number down.
ring._iconSize: Never below 40. Under it the 256px source is minified past 6x and the painted outlines break up — the same failure the whole cast had before rule 7 was restated in physical pixels.
ring._panelMinWidth: The narrowest the description panel may be squeezed to. It takes the widest width that fits BESIDE the ring, down to this, so that on a small screen the panel stops sitting on top of the ring's own buttons — a covered button costs a tap every time, cancel back to the ring and then press it, and the smallest screen is the one a kid is most likely holding. Measured: at 844x390 a 200px panel hides nothing at all, and at a notched 568x320 narrowing from 226 takes the worst case from four buttons hidden to two and the number of placements that hide any from 225 of 540 down to 55. Below about 150 the stat rows start colliding with their own values.
ring._panelWidth: Fixed. Text wraps into it; the panel never widens to fit a long name, because a panel whose width depends on its content moves the confirm button between towers.
ring._bodyMinSize: The floor the description shrinks to. Below this it is not small text, it is a grey smear on a phone. If the content still does not fit at this size the panel SAYS SO rather than clipping.
ring._maxAspect: The HUD leaves a wide, short strip — 824x210 on the reference phone — and a circle big enough to keep six plates apart is 242px in both directions. The ring stretches sideways into the room that is actually there, up to this, and no further: past it the ring stops reading as a ring and starts reading as a row.
ring._rowMinHeight: Stat rows tighten with the description when a panel is too tall. A support tower spends more height on rows than on prose, so shrinking only the prose is not enough of a lever.
ring._headerIconSize: The picture at the top of the description panel, so the player can see which ring button they are reading about. Smaller than iconSize deliberately: that 40px floor is for buttons a thumb has to hit, and this one is not pressed. The 14px it gives back is the difference between the panel fitting a notched phone and reporting that it does not.
ring._confirmHeight: Tall enough to actually carry a 40px icon. It was 38, which is shorter than the icon standing on it — the floor is a floor, and a plate that cannot hold it is the plate that has to grow.
ring._titleMinSize: The title gives way last, because it is what a player reads first — but two lines of 16px title is 40px of a 238px budget on the smallest phone.
ring._arcMaxOptions: At or below this many options the ring is not a ring: the buttons go on a tight arc directly against the pad instead. Fitting an ellipse to two options puts them at top and bottom and then grows the radius until the plates separate, which is a 50x194 vertical column — a line, not a ring, and 124px of empty space between two buttons about the same pad. The loadout hands out two towers, so this is the NORMAL case rather than an edge one.
ring._arcSpreadDeg: How wide the tight arc fans. Wide enough that two 50px plates separate at a radius that still hugs the anchor, narrow enough that the group reads as one thing sitting above the pad rather than as buttons scattered around it.
ring._lockBadgeSize: The padlock corner-badge on an option the player cannot afford yet. Small, because it is the second thing the button says: the first is WHICH option this is, and that is the option's own picture, dimmed. A padlock instead of the picture was the original choice and the reasoning held for one locked option — a padlock says 'not yet' where a greyed-out picture just looks broken. It fails at two, because then both buttons are the same padlock and the player cannot tell what they are saving for, which is the common case.
ring._confirmGlyphMinWidth: Below this the confirm button carries its word alone; at or above it the tick glyph goes in front of the word too. The word is the part that cannot be dropped — every option's confirm used to be the same tick, so SELL and UPGRADE committed through identical buttons.

ledger._note: The one card. Four rows, a fixed height, no prose. It replaces a bevelled nine-slice plate carrying a title, a paragraph, five stat rows and a cost row — plus a four-step ladder (body size, row height, title size, then drop the prose) that existed only to make the paragraph fit and made the card's height depend on how long a sentence was.
ledger._statChangedSize: Smaller than a plain value, because the upgrade state puts two numbers where one usually goes.
ledger._minStatWidth: Below this a column cannot hold a value over its label, so the third number goes. At the 150px floor the inner width is 126, which is two columns.
ledger._primary: A solid muted green with a darker bottom band. Not a bevel: one edge, no highlight, no gradient.

settings._note: The settings dialog: three volume sliders and the three ways out of a run. It replaced a mute toggle with a stepped volume readout in one corner and a pause button in the other — four controls' worth of chrome on a phone screen, for settings that are opened once and left alone. Everything here is in CSS pixels and clamped to the viewport.
settings._handleRadius: 22px across. The smallest thing a thumb can reliably grab is about 44px, and the handle is not the hit area: the whole ROW takes the drag, so a press anywhere along the track moves the handle to it. The circle only has to be visible.
settings._width: Clamped to the viewport, so on a 568x320 screen it is the screen minus its margins rather than 420. minWidth is where the label, the track and the percentage stop fitting on one line.
settings._labelColumn: Room reserved for a row's name, so the three tracks start in one column whatever the words are. Measured against SOUND EFFECTS, the longest, at labelSize with its letter spacing: it was 118 and the words ran under the track.

cutscene._note: The comic's layout. A band is RESERVED out of the safe area for SKIP and the panel counter, and the panel is contain-fitted into what is left -- so the controls are never on the art, which a corner placement cannot promise at 16:9 where there is no letterbox band to sit in. Which edge the band comes off is measured rather than chosen: both are fitted and the larger panel wins. skipWidth/skipHeight are POINTS and 44 is the floor; a test holds them there.

heroFx._note: HOW THE TEN HERO POWERS DRAW THEMSELVES. This block was the placeholder art itself -- ring widths, fill alphas and tooth counts for five procedural shapes -- and it is now the numbers that FIT REAL PICTURES to the powers. The rule that survived the swap is the one that mattered: nothing invents a size, every effect is scaled to the radius, reach or corridor the power actually uses (heroes.json), so tuning a radius moves its picture with it. See systems/HeroFx.ts.
heroFx._growFrom: An effect ARRIVES at its size rather than appearing at it, which is the one idea kept from the expanding ring it replaces: a picture that grows into place is what makes the extent legible in the half second it is up.
heroFx._seismicFlatten: fx_seismic is drawn HEAD-ON and the board is seen from three quarters above, so at 1:1 it reads as a wall of rock standing up out of the map rather than as a crater lying flat on it. 0.62 is the same foreshortening the painted map uses on its own ground detail. It is a per-effect number because it is a fact about how that one picture was drawn.
heroFx._beamHeight: THE BEAM'S THICKNESS IS NOT ITS POWER'S RADIUS, and this is the one effect where the two come apart. Ice Beam's `radius` is the 96px area that freezes at the far end; the line drawn from Eli to that point is scenery and touches nothing it crosses, which a test enforces. Drawing the picture 192px thick would say the whole corridor was caught. 54 reads as a beam. The AREA still gets a ring at its true radius on top -- see `areaRing` -- because a fixed-thickness picture cannot say how big a circle is, and that circle is what the power was tuned against.
heroFx._markerHeight: Status markers -- the flame over a burning enemy, and the marker over a controlled one -- in world pixels, and how far above the enemy's head they float. Small: a marker the size of the enemy is a second enemy.
heroFx._strikeArtWidth: Each of Star Rain's fourteen strikes is drawn `strikeLength` x this wide, so the picture covers the 26px disc that strike actually damages with enough overhang to read as a falling star rather than as a dot. The volley is fourteen small pictures, not one big one, because THE SCATTER IS THE POWER: one image over the whole radius would say a blast landed.
heroFx._retired: GONE WITH THE PLACEHOLDER SHAPES: ringMs, ringWidth, fillAlpha, rainRingMs, strikeMs, strikeWidth, hazardThickness, hazardTeeth and hazardToothHeight. They described a stroked circle, a two-line stab and a toothed rectangle, and there is real art in all three places now. `strikeLength` STAYED and is not one of them -- it is the 26px radius a single Star Rain strike actually damages, a gameplay number that the picture is now sized against rather than a property of the picture.

targeting._note: What the board looks like while it is waiting for a tap. On a touch device there is no hover, so a targeting mode that only draws under the pointer draws NOTHING until the player has already committed — which is how a mode with no visible state came to be reported as a soft-lock. These numbers are the standing affordance: a breathing wash over the area a tap is legal in, drawn from the moment the mode is entered.

castCursor._note: Where a summon will land, drawn under the pointer instead of as an outline down both edges of the whole lane. The band described the RULE; the cursor answers the QUESTION, which is 'can I drop it here?'. Kingdom Rush draws nothing on the map.
castCursor._size: World pixels at zoom 1. The cursor divides by the camera zoom, so this is also its size on the glass at every camera position.
castCursor._stub: Tinted rectangles stand in until the two sprites arrive. Deliberately crude: a stub that looks finished is a stub that ships. The real art replaces it by dropping files in under the two keys above, with no code change.

bossCard._note: The card that announces a boss. Sized from its own text: it was drawn at exactly the viewport width and 156px tall, which is 40% of a 390px phone, for a two-word name and one line of flavour.
bossCard._sizes: 44 over 21 is 2.1:1. It was 56 over 17, which is 3.3:1 — at that ratio the tagline reads as a caption rather than as part of the card.
bossCard._maxWidthFraction: The screen is the bound, not the size. A card may reach 82% of the width and no further, so it is always a card on a plate rather than a band across the screen.

heroPick._note: How big a tap on the hero has to be. Derived from the sprite he is currently wearing, not from a constant: it was a hardcoded radius of 30 around his FEET, which reached 40% up a 75.8px-tall man and thirty pixels down into the grass below him.
heroPick._marginFraction: Grown by this much on every side, so the box is larger than the sprite as asked. 18% of 75.8 is about 14 world pixels of forgiveness top and bottom, which is roughly a fingertip at the default zoom.
heroPick._min: A floor in world pixels, so a small or a shrunken sprite still gets a target a finger can hit.

banner._note: The one-at-a-time banner across the board. There was no queue and no slot: every call made a new text at the same pixel, and endWave fires NEW TOWER and WAVE CLEARED zero milliseconds apart, so the two were drawn through each other.
banner._gapMs: Between one banner leaving and the next arriving, so two in a row read as two messages rather than as one flicker.

drawer._note: The opt-in control drawer, behind the save flag `controlDrawer`. A tab docked to the right edge that expands a panel of tiles. First slice: the six active units only — no passives, no consumables, no upgrade screen.
drawer._widths: ONE BREAKPOINT CARRIES THE WHOLE BUDGET, not just the width. The panel is 200px tall at 844x390 and only 130 at 568x320 — the HUD rows above and the ability strip below decide that, not this file — so a header, a tab bar and a detail strip at one set of heights leave 18px of grid on the narrow screen, which is less than half a tile and therefore no tappable tile at all. The narrow row is the same layout with every piece of chrome cut to what it actually needs. Widest first; the last must be minViewW 0 so there is always an answer.
drawer._iconFraction: How much of a tile's height the artwork takes. The rest is the price.
drawer._lockFill: A light bone padlock over the dimmed art. It used to be drawn in COLOR.panelEdge — 0x3d4a59, the old bevelled-plate blue — on a 0x4a3a2a tile, which rendered every frame and was invisible in every screenshot.
drawer._dimAlpha: A tile the player cannot afford. Dimmed, not hidden: what you are saving for is information.
drawer._outline: Thick and dark, matching the painted board. Flat colour, chunky rounded forms — no bevel, no metal, no neon edge, no gradient, no translucent hairline. The reference is the in-game side drawer, not a web panel.
drawer._dragSlop: How far a finger may travel before a press becomes a drag rather than a pick. Below this the tap selects on release; above it the grid scrolls and nothing is selected.
drawer._scrollbar: Shown only when the grid actually scrolls. Without it, at 568x320, two of the six towers are off the bottom of a panel that looks complete.
drawer._nodeRing: A highlight PAINTED ON THE GROUND, not a decal laid over it. Two passes: a dark under-stroke first, then the warm ochre on top of it, the way a painted line on dirt has a shadow in the groove it sits in. The dark pass is what makes it hold up on light dirt and where it crosses the road, which a single bright stroke did not. IT WAS INVISIBLE BEFORE THIS. Measured on the plate, the previous settings lifted the channels by about 8-12 levels above the surrounding grass and needed roughly 5x amplification to be seen in analysis at all. That was an overcorrection from the flat 0xffd23f decal before it: the edge went from a full-strength 3px rim to 0.55 alpha at 2px, which is the other ditch. The lever is these six numbers and not the shape.
drawer._nodePulse: How a build node says it will take the selected tower. A scale beat rather than a colour flash: the pads are already tinted three ways and a fourth tint would be a colour nobody can name. The alphas and BOTH stroke widths beat with the scale, because a pulse that only moves the radius by a fifth of a stroke width is a change of almost nothing into almost nothing.
drawer._tabLabels: Only the first is populated. ACTIVE and PASSIVE render as disabled tabs so that filling them later is data rather than a layout change, which is the whole reason the bar exists now. A label that will not fit is replaced by a drawn glyph rather than truncated: "TOWE..." is worse than a picture.
drawer._detail: The strip is PINNED at the bottom and reserves its height whether or not anything is selected. Collapsing it when empty would re-flow the grid under the finger at the exact moment a tile has just been tapped, which is how mis-taps are made. Empty means blank, not absent.
drawer._tabLabelSize: Requested, not rendered. `uiSize` clamps every screen-space size up to typography.minUiSize, which is 15, so a tab label draws at 15 however small a number is put here. That clamp is the reason the words do not fit: "TOWERS" at 15px bold is 71px wide and the widest tab this drawer has is 44. The brief expected "about 43px is enough for a short word at small caps"; it is not, against this project’s own legibility floor, so the glyph fallback the brief specified for the narrow screen is what runs on both. Lowering this number changes nothing; lowering minUiSize would trade the drawer’s tabs against every other piece of small UI in the game.
drawer._detailSizes: ALL THREE ARE THE FLOOR, and they have to be. typography.minUiSize is 15 and `uiSize` clamps every screen-space size up to it, so "small labels" under the numbers is not a thing this strip can have: three captions at 15px need about 100px and the text column is 92 at 844x390 and 68 at 568x320. What the strip carries is therefore the name, the three numbers in a fixed order, and the trait where there is room for it — see reports/ for the arithmetic and the three ways out.

worldMap._note: THE ROAD ON THE LEVEL-SELECT SCREEN, and every number that shapes it. The screen used to be four full-size cards scattered across the design box at hand-authored positions: it had run out of room at four levels, the cards were different apparent sizes because the pictures were, and the path drawn between them in level order ran the width of the screen backwards. It is one winding road of identical nodes now, laid out by level order, long enough to carry every planned level -- so it is wider than the design box and scrolls sideways.
worldMap._band: The vertical space the road may use, in design units: under the title and above the scrollbar. The wave is centred so that the DEEPEST node's name still lands inside it, which is what puts the road in the middle of the screen instead of in the top half with the bottom empty.
worldMap._node: IDENTICAL FOR EVERY LEVEL, built and unbuilt alike -- which is the fix for four cards that read as four different sizes. 160x107 is 3:2, the aspect the card art is cropped at, so no picture is stretched to fit. `framePad` is the painted border, and it is the border rather than the picture that has to clear the next node.
worldMap._pitch: Distance between node centres along the road, and the side margin at each end of it. 210 against a 168-wide framed node leaves 42 units of road showing between neighbours, and holds two names apart at the narrowest viewport the game runs at.
worldMap._sway: The road's wave: a node's centre is `centre + amplitude * sin(index * step)`. The step is deliberately not a neat fraction of a turn, so the road does not repeat itself over twenty nodes and no two neighbours land at the same height. The amplitude is as large as the band allows once the longest name and its unlock line are reserved for.
worldMap._label: The name under a node, wrapped to the node's width. `reserve` is the room kept for it when the road is centred, and it is MEASURED off a rendered frame rather than counted in lines: SPORTS COMPLEX AT DUSK wraps to three lines and its unlock line to two, which comes to 147 design units, and that is the worst case any node can be. A short reserve does not clip the text -- it pushes the deepest node down until its last line lands under the scrollbar, which is exactly what a first pass at 118 did. 22 is the floor for a screen that is fitted from the design box down onto a phone; below it this text is seven real pixels.
worldMap._badge: The level number, top-left of every node. It is the one thing on the screen that says where in the campaign a node sits, which is the whole point of a road.
worldMap._path: The road: a bed, a lighter surface over it, and evenly spaced steps along the middle, drawn as ONE polyline through every node in level order. It passes BEHIND the nodes, which is what makes it read as a single road rather than as a set of links between cards.
worldMap._scrollbar: SHOWN ONLY WHEN THE ROAD IS LONGER THAN THE SCREEN, and horizontal, because that is the axis the road runs on. Drawn rather than made a control: the map itself is dragged, so the bar reports where you are and there is no thin target to miss.
worldMap._states: THREE, AND THEY HAVE TO BE TELLABLE APART AT A GLANCE. cleared: full colour, a green frame, a tick. open: full colour, an amber frame and a ring, nothing over the picture -- this is the one to play. locked: the picture darkened to a cool grey under a padlock, or a bare plate where the level is not built yet.
worldMap._plate: The node's own backing, which every node has and only an unbuilt one shows: a level that is not built yet has no picture to crop a card from, so its slot is the plate, the number on its badge, a padlock and `unbuiltLabel`. The label is there because a padlock alone reads as YOU HAVE NOT EARNED THIS when the truth is THIS DOES NOT EXIST YET, and a player who reads the first goes looking for what they missed. Sixteen invented level names would be inventing the campaign, so it carries none.
worldMap._lockHeight: The padlock over a locked node, as a fraction of the node's height.
worldMap._ring: The pulse around the one level that is open and unplayed. It is the only thing on the screen that moves, so it cannot be missed and nothing else competes with it.

safeArea._housingAtAngle90: Which horizontal edge the sensor housing lands on at screen.orientation.angle 90, which is landscape-primary. That is iOS landscapeLeft — home indicator on the right, device top edge on the left — so the housing is on the left, and 270 is the mirror of it. THIS IS THE ONE VALUE HERE NOT VERIFIED ON HARDWARE: it comes from the orientation conventions, not from a notched phone. Both branches are tested and both viewports are asserted; if the inset ever shows up on the wrong edge, flip this string and change nothing else.

heroBarFade._note: THE FLOATING BAR OVER THE HERO'S HEAD, which is up only while he is damaged. In fast and out slow: the fade IN has to keep up with the hit that caused it, and the fade OUT is the board going quiet again and should not snatch the bar away the instant a heal or a revive lands. Tweened rather than toggled because an element that blinks on and off over a moving sprite reads as a rendering fault.
